objective: AQA Chemistry bond wording and evidence-first mock-only revision

status.notes: Earlier v153 checklist statuses are historical assessments; new questions improve application evidence without certifying complete coverage, and overlapping core recall remains.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why is benzene more stable than a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene?
editedCards.oldBack: Its π electrons are delocalised around the ring, lowering the energy.
editedCards.front: Why is benzene more stable than a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene?
editedCards.back: Delocalised electrons are spread around the ring, lowering its energy.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why are benzene C–C bonds equal in length?
editedCards.oldBack: The π electrons are delocalised around the aromatic ring.
editedCards.front: Why are benzene C–C bonds equal in length?
editedCards.back: Delocalised electrons are shared around the ring.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What happens to the C=O π electron pair during initial attack?
editedCards.oldBack: It temporarily moves towards oxygen.
editedCards.front: What happens to the C=O bonding electron pair during initial attack?
editedCards.back: It moves towards the oxygen atom.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What change restores the carbonyl during the elimination stage?
editedCards.oldBack: An oxygen lone pair reforms the C=O π bond.
editedCards.front: What change reforms C=O during the elimination stage?
editedCards.back: An oxygen lone pair reforms the carbon–oxygen double bond.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Which bond makes an alkene rich in electrons?
editedCards.oldBack: The π bond of the carbon–carbon double bond.
editedCards.front: Why is an alkene's C=C bond attractive to electrophiles?
editedCards.back: The double bond is a region of high electron density.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What is the source of the first electron-pair arrow in electrophilic addition?
editedCards.oldBack: The alkene π bond.
editedCards.front: Where does the first curly arrow start in alkene electrophilic addition?
editedCards.back: At the electron-rich C=C double bond.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Where do carbonyl π electrons go in nucleophilic addition?
editedCards.oldBack: Toward oxygen while a new bond to carbon forms.
editedCards.front: Where do the C=O bonding electrons move during nucleophilic addition?
editedCards.back: Towards oxygen while the incoming group bonds to carbon.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What type of bonds occur in alkanes?
editedCards.oldBack: Single covalent σ bonds.
editedCards.front: What carbon–carbon bonds occur in alkanes?
editedCards.back: Only single covalent bonds.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Which part of a C=C bond is attacked in electrophilic addition?
editedCards.oldBack: The electron-rich π bond.
editedCards.front: Which part of an alkene reacts with an electrophile?
editedCards.back: Its electron-rich C=C double bond.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What is delocalisation in benzene?
editedCards.oldBack: π electrons are spread over the ring rather than fixed between pairs.
editedCards.front: What is delocalisation in benzene?
editedCards.back: Electrons are shared across the benzene ring rather than fixed between pairs of atoms.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?
editedCards.oldBack: Addition would disrupt the stable delocalised π system.
editedCards.front: Why does benzene favour substitution over addition?
editedCards.back: Addition would disrupt benzene's stable delocalised electron ring.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What makes a carbon–carbon double bond electron-rich?
editedCards.oldBack: Its π bond electrons.
editedCards.front: Why is an alkene's carbon–carbon double bond electron-rich?
editedCards.back: It contains an electron pair available for electrophilic addition.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What happens to the π bond during electrophilic addition?
editedCards.oldBack: It breaks as new σ bonds form.
editedCards.front: What happens to the C=C bond during electrophilic addition?
editedCards.back: It becomes a single bond as new bonds form to the carbons.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: What makes benzene especially stable?
editedCards.oldBack: Delocalisation of π electrons around the ring.
editedCards.front: What makes benzene especially stable?
editedCards.back: Delocalised electrons around the benzene ring lower its energy.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why is the alkene double bond attacked by electrophiles?
editedCards.oldBack: The π bond has high electron density.
editedCards.front: Why is the alkene double bond attacked by electrophiles?
editedCards.back: The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why does benzene react by substitution rather than addition?
editedCards.oldBack: Substitution retains its delocalised π-electron ring.
editedCards.front: Why does benzene react by substitution rather than addition?
editedCards.back: Substitution retains the stable delocalised electrons in the ring.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why are the six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene equal in length?
editedCards.oldBack: The π electrons are delocalised across the ring.
editedCards.front: Why are the six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene equal in length?
editedCards.back: Electrons are delocalised across all six carbon atoms.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: An alkene C=C consists of which two bond types?
editedCards.oldBack: One σ bond and one π bond.
editedCards.front: How does AQA describe the bonding in an alkene?
editedCards.back: A C=C double covalent bond that is a centre of high electron density.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why does a C=C bond restrict rotation?
editedCards.oldBack: Rotation would disrupt sideways overlap forming the π bond.
editedCards.front: What structural feature of C=C makes E/Z isomerism possible?
editedCards.back: Rotation around a C=C double bond is restricted.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Why does Br₂ become polarised as it approaches an alkene?
editedCards.oldBack: The alkene π electrons repel Br₂ electrons, inducing a dipole.
editedCards.front: Why does Br₂ become polarised as it approaches an alkene?
editedCards.back: The electron-rich C=C bond repels Br₂ electrons, inducing a dipole.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: Br₂ addition arrow 1: where do the alkene π electrons move?
editedCards.oldBack: Towards the induced δ⁺ bromine atom.
editedCards.front: In Br₂ addition, where does the first arrow from C=C point?
editedCards.back: To the bromine atom with induced δ⁺ charge.

editedCards.subject: Chemistry
editedCards.oldFront: During alcohol dehydration, which electrons form the alkene's π bond?
editedCards.oldBack: A pair from a C–H bond next to the carbon losing water.
editedCards.front: During alcohol dehydration, which electrons form the new C=C bond?
editedCards.back: Electrons from a C–H bond on the adjacent carbon.

addedCards.front: Name one use of superconductors in the AQA specification.
addedCards.back: Strong magnetic fields or lower energy losses in power transmission.

addedCards.front: Why can a superconducting power cable reduce heating losses?
addedCards.back: It has zero electrical resistance below its critical temperature.

addedCards.front: What happens to resistance when a load is added in parallel?
addedCards.back: The combined resistance of that branch decreases.

addedCards.front: Why can loading the lower part of a divider lower its output voltage?
addedCards.back: The parallel load lowers that branch resistance and its share of the supply p.d.
